title: Dot Product of Mostly-Zero Vectors
statement:
Two vectors a and b have the same length, and most of their entries are zero. Return their dot product: the sum of a[i] · b[i] over all positions i.

In an interview this usually comes as a class: the constructor receives the full array once and stores it in a compact form, and a dotProduct(other) method multiplies two such objects many times. Here both arrays come in one call, but the point is the same. Store only the non-zero entries as (index, value) pairs, and compute the product from those pairs so that the work depends on the number of non-zeros, not on the length.

examples.why: Only position 1 is non-zero in both: 4 · 5 = 20. The 2 and the 1 sit at different positions and contribute nothing.
The non-zeros never line up, so every product is 0.
1·2 + 3·3 + 2·4 = 2 + 9 + 8. A long dense vector against a sparse one still only needs the sparse one's positions.

hints: Positions where either vector is zero add nothing. Which positions actually matter?
Turn each vector into a list of (index, value) pairs for the non-zero entries. These lists come out sorted by index.
Walk both pair lists with two pointers, like merging sorted lists. Multiply when the indexes match, otherwise advance the pointer with the smaller index.

explain.intuition:
A product a[i] · b[i] is non-zero only when both entries are non-zero. So the only positions worth visiting are the ones in both vectors' non-zero sets. Storing each vector as a sorted list of (index, value) pairs makes this an intersection of two sorted lists, which two pointers handle in one pass.

It is the same reason a virtual list in a UI stores only rows that exist: memory and time follow the data, not the nominal size. If one vector is far sparser than the other, binary-searching its indexes in the other list is even faster.
steps: Build pa: the (i, a[i]) pairs with a[i] ≠ 0, in index order. Build pb the same way.
While both pointers are inside their lists: if the indexes are equal, add the product and advance both.
Otherwise advance the pointer whose index is smaller.
pitfalls: Storing pairs in a hash map and then looping over the full length anyway. That keeps the memory saving but loses the time saving.
Advancing the wrong pointer when indexes differ. Always move the smaller one, or you skip matches.
Dropping zero entries from only one vector. Both compact forms must keep their original indexes, not positions in the compact list.

complexity.time: O(n) to build the pairs, then O(p + q) per product for p and q non-zeros

solutions.title: Dense loop
solutions.idea: Multiply position by position. Correct, but it does not use the sparsity at all.

solutions.title: Hash map of non-zeros
solutions.idea: Store one vector as index → value, then walk the other's non-zeros and look each index up.

solutions.title: Sorted pairs, two pointers
solutions.idea: Compress both vectors into index-sorted (index, value) pairs and intersect them like a merge.

followups: One vector has 10 non-zeros and the other has a million. How do you exploit that? (Hint: binary search.)
Why might an interviewer object to the hash-map version? Think about hashing cost and memory compared with a sorted array of pairs.
